item.title: C2 moving material circuit: swept patch, single-valued material velocity, flux and electromotive force
item.statement:
Let the laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ and its inertial chart, the field objects $E,B$ and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], with $c>0$.

(a) [Moving material circuit] A moving material circuit on the laboratory region is the data $(D,r,v)$ specified as follows. $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a compact finite elementary Green region with its positive boundary orientation; $r:D\times I\to\Omega$ extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ and $r(\cdot,t)$ injective on the interior of $D$ for every $t$ (embedded material sheet); and $v$ is a $C^1$ vector field on a neighbourhood of the swept set $\{(r(u,w,t),t):(u,w)\in D,\ t\in I\}$ in $\Omega\times I$ satisfying the single-valued condition $v(r(u,w,t),t)=\partial_tr(u,w,t)$ for all $(u,w)\in D$ and all $t\in I$. In the notation of [[def-em-moving-patch]] the map $r$ is the swept moving patch and $v$ is its single-valued velocity; material points of the circuit are the images of the parameter points $(u,w)$.

(b) [Surface, boundary and flux] For $t\in I$ put $S(t):=r(D,t)$ and let $C(t):=\partial S(t)$ carry the boundary orientation induced by the positive orientation of $D$. For $B$ of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the magnetic flux of the circuit at time $t$ is the parametrized flux
$$\Phi_B(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(u,w,t),t),\,r_u(u,w,t)\times r_v(u,w,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dw$$
of [[def-em-moving-patch]]; its unit is the weber, $\mathrm{Wb}=\mathrm T\,\mathrm m^2$.

(c) [Electromotive force] For $E,B$ continuous on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the electromotive force (emf) of the circuit at time $t$ is the vector line integral over the oriented closed path $C(t)$
$$\mathrm{emf}(t):=\oint_{C(t)}\bigl\langle E(\cdot,t)+v(\cdot,t)\times B(\cdot,t),\,d\mathbf r\bigr\rangle$$
in the convention of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]], with the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; its unit is the volt, $1\,\mathrm V=1\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-3}\mathrm A^{-1}$. Under the framework's Lorentz coupling the integrand is the force per unit charge on a charge moving with the conductor material; the definition itself only names the line integral.

(d) [Scope and exclusions] The fields are assumed of the stated regularity on a neighbourhood of the swept set: circuits passing through a point charge, a curve or surface singularity, or any place where the fields fail to be of that regularity are excluded (no singularity crossings). When the emf is interpreted through the framework's relativistic Lorentz coupling, material speeds are required to be subluminal, $|v|<c$. The definition asserts no conservation law and no relation between $\mathrm{emf}$ and $\Phi_B'$; in particular the flux concerns the single field $B$ and the emf the pair $(E,B)$, and neither object is claimed independent of the chosen parametrization.
item.strategy: Explicit type/domain/convention definition. The integrand of $\Phi_B$ is continuous on the compact parameter region $D$ because $B$ and $r$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ and $r_u,r_v$ are continuous; the flux is therefore a Riemann integral over a compact Jordan-measurable region in the moving-patch convention of [[def-em-moving-patch]]. The line integral is taken in the piecewise $C^1$ path convention of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]; the $C^2$ extension of $r$ and the single-valued $C^1$ condition on $v$ are exactly the hypotheses under which the moving-patch definition and its transport lemma are stated. Clause (d) records the no-singularity-crossing hypothesis and the subluminal condition; neither is used in the definition of the flux itself. No physical assertion beyond the definition is made, and no proof is claimed.

item.title: Symmetry and Fubini representation of the Newtonian linkage pairing
item.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the Tonelli, Fubini and polar/kernel-local-integrability interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $N$ be the Newtonian potential transform of [[def-newtonian-potential]], so that for real $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
and let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ be the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For $u,v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ write $Nu:=(Nu_1,Nu_2,Nu_3)$ componentwise, so that the linkage pairing is the map
$$B(u,v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x).$$
Then all three integrals
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle Nu(x),v(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)$$
converge absolutely ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]) and have the same value; therefore $B$ is well defined, real-valued, symmetric, $B(u,v)=B(v,u)$, and bilinear over $\mathbb R$ in each argument. In particular the common value of the three integrals is unchanged by exchanging the two density fields $u$ and $v$ and the two integration variables.
item.strategy: **Proof technique:** absolute convergence on a compact product, then Tonelli and Fubini. 1.1 Both supports lie in a closed ball $\overline B_R(0)$; on the product $\overline B_R(0)\times\overline B_R(0)$ the kernel $|x-y|^{-1}$ is locally integrable ([[lem-laplace-fundamental-kernel-is-locally-integrable]] for the normalised kernel, whose singularity is $|z|^{-1}$ in dimension three), and $|\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle|\le\|u\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); Tonelli's theorem ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) applied to the nonnegative integrand $|\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle|/|x-y|$ shows that the iterated integral $\int\int|\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle|/|x-y|\,d\lambda_3(y)d\lambda_3(x)$ is finite, so the double integral converges absolutely and Fubini ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) computes it as either iterated integral. 1.2 Since $Nv$ is well defined by the same compactness and local integrability ([[def-newtonian-potential]]), the first two integrals equal the double integral by the definition of $N$ and Fubini again; the constant $1/(4\pi)$ is the normalisation of the kernel. 1.3 Exchanging the names of the two variables $(x,y)$ in the absolutely convergent double integral leaves its value unchanged, which gives $B(u,v)=B(v,u)$; linearity in each slot follows by applying [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]] to the inner integral and then to the outer integral. Countable Choice is inherited only through the Tonelli/Fubini and local-integrability interfaces; no stronger choice principle is used.

after.strategy:
Absolute convergence first, then Fubini. Choose $R>0$ such that both supports are contained in the open ball $B_R(0)$. Assign $g(0)=0$ and $g(z)=|z|^{-1}$ otherwise. This is Borel, and the kernel-local-integrability supplier [[lem-laplace-fundamental-kernel-is-locally-integrable]] gives $K_R:=\int_{B_{2R}}g(z)d\lambda_3(z)<\infty$. For each $x\in B_R$, the translation $z=x-y$ carries $B_R$ into $B_{2R}$ and has absolute Jacobian one. The actual $L^1$ change-of-variables formula [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]], applied to the restriction $g\mathbf1_{B_{2R}}$, therefore gives $\int_{B_R}g(x-y)dy\le K_R$. Hence
$$\int_{B_R}\int_{B_R}g(x-y)dy\,dx\le\lambda_3(B_R)K_R<\infty.$$
The ball has finite measure by [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]], and the bound uses [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]. The product integrand is Borel: subtraction is continuous, the assigned kernel is Borel and the smooth density factors are Borel. Under [[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]], its Euclidean and product-measure interpretations agree; in particular it is measurable for the product sigma-algebra, so [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] applies before finiteness has been established. Multiplying the displayed bound by $\|u\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty$ proves absolute finiteness of $\iint\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle/(4\pi|x-y|)$ (with assigned diagonal value), and [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] permits either order. For any fixed $x$, compact bounded $v$ has an everywhere-finite Newtonian integral: choose a ball containing $x-\operatorname{supp}v$ and bound the translated kernel integral there as above. The same estimate applies to $u$. Thus the pointwise $Nu,Nv$ of [[def-newtonian-potential]] are legitimate, and $|u\cdot Nv|\le\int |u(x)|\,|v(y)|g(x-y)/(4\pi)dy$ makes both outer pairings integrable by the already-proved bound ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]] componentwise). Fubini identifies them with the common double integral. Exchanging the variables gives symmetry because $g(x-y)=g(y-x)$ and the Euclidean pairing is symmetric; finite linearity of the two integrals gives bilinearity ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). The arbitrary diagonal assignment changes each section only at one null point and does not change these integrals, as in the Newtonian/kernel interfaces. The choice cost is exactly the declared AComega of the translated Lebesgue, ball, kernel and product-measure interfaces.

item.title: Curl-field energy identity for Newtonian potentials of divergence-free compact currents
item.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the Newtonian, polar and Lebesgue interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mu_0>0$ be a real scalar parameter, let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]), and define componentwise
$$A:=\mu_0N(J),\qquad A_i=\mu_0\,N(J_i),\qquad N f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
the Newtonian vector potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]]. Then:
(a) $A\in C^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}A=0$ and $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$, componentwise ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]);
(b) there is $C>0$ with $|\operatorname{curl}A(x)|\le C/(1+|x|^2)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$; hence $\operatorname{curl}A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\langle A,J\rangle\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$, both in the ordinary Lebesgue sense ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]);
(c) the curl-field energy identity
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3=\mu_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3$$
holds, and equivalently $\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3\ge0$.
The identity is stated for the explicit smooth compact currents and the Newtonian construction; no uniqueness, no decay of $A$ itself beyond the curl bound of (b), and no extension to singular currents is claimed.

item.title: Moving-loop electromotive force equals the negative flux derivative
item.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]], inherited from the Maxwell and transport suppliers below. Let $\Omega\times I$ be the laboratory region with $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0$, $\mu_0$ the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $E,B$ be fields and $\rho,J$ source fields of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], jointly of class $C^2$ and $C^1$ respectively on $\Omega\times I$, satisfying the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell equations pointwise on $\Omega\times I$. Let $(D,r,v)$ be a moving material circuit of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]] with time interval $I$, and fix a compact subinterval $J\subseteq I$ such that the swept set $r(D\times J)$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$ (no singularity crossing). Put $S(t)=r(D,t)$, $C(t)=\partial S(t)$ with the induced orientation.

Then the flux $\Phi_B:I\to\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]] is differentiable at every $t\in I$ with
$$\Phi_B'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{C(t)}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$
for every $t\in J$ the frozen patch $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ is a test geometry of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], the fixed-patch Faraday identity
$$\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS=-\oint_{C(t)}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$$
holds, and consequently the electromotive force of the circuit satisfies
$$\mathrm{emf}(t)=\oint_{C(t)}(E+v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\Phi_B'(t)\qquad\text{for every }t\in J.$$
The physical reading, under the adopted coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], is that the work per unit charge of the electromagnetic force on charges moving with the conductor material equals minus the rate of change of the magnetic flux through the circuit. The result is conditional on the joint regularity, the smooth Maxwell branch and the no-singularity-crossing hypothesis; it asserts no fixed-loop formula for arbitrary moving loops, no field uniqueness, no statement about singular supports and no empirical claim.
item.strategy: **Proof technique:** the flux-transport lemma of the research route [[lem-em-moving-flux]], the frozen-patch Faraday clause of [[pthm-em-integral-maxwell]], and linearity of the line integral. 1.1 The hypotheses of the moving-patch definition are met: $D$ is a compact finite elementary Green region, $r$ extends $C^2$ to a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$, and $v$ is single-valued of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set ([[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]]); $B$ is $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set and $\operatorname{div}B=0$ holds pointwise (smooth Maxwell branch), so [[lem-em-moving-flux]] gives differentiability of $\Phi_B$ and the displayed transport formula. 1.2 Fix $t\in J$ and freeze the patch: $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ is a fixed oriented regular $C^2$ patch over the elementary region $D$ with a neighbourhood on which $E,B$ are $C^2$ and the smooth Maxwell equations hold, hence a test geometry of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]; the differential-to-integral clause of [[pthm-em-integral-maxwell]] applied to it gives the fixed-patch Faraday identity, the flux function being differentiable with derivative $\int_S\partial_tB\cdot n$ by the same clause. 1.3 Add the two integrals: by linearity and concatenation of vector line integrals ([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]), $\oint_C(E+v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r=\oint_CE\cdot d\mathbf r+\oint_C(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$, and substituting steps 1.1 and 1.2 at $t$ gives $\operatorname{emf}(t)=-\Phi_B'(t)$. The Lorentz-force interpretation of the integrand is the adopted coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] and is not used in the algebraic identity itself. Countable Choice is inherited from [[pthm-em-integral-maxwell]] and [[lem-em-moving-flux]]; no stronger choice principle is used.

item.title: Electro- and magneto-quasistatic lumped circuit model
item.statement:
Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following reduced circuit description, to be used only within its declared regime. Let the laboratory region, its chart and units and the compact smooth current class be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], and let the material response be one of the branches of [[post-em-material-closure]].

(a) [Circuit data] Fix a finite set of branches $\alpha=1,\dots,n$ (and capacitive branches $\beta=1,\dots,m$) and a time interval $J$. The model carries branch currents $I_\alpha:J\to\mathbb R$, branch charges $Q_\beta:J\to\mathbb R$, terminal potentials $V_\alpha:J\to\mathbb R$, and constant matrices $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ and $R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, with $L$ and $C$ symmetric, $C$ positive definite and $R$ symmetric positive semidefinite. The matrices, the terminal geometry and the choice of independent loops are fixed data of the model; they are declared, not derived here, and the smooth compact-current realization of the inductive couplings and its reciprocity are analysed separately on this page.

(b) [Branch relations and network laws] In the declared regime the inductive branches obey the Faraday branch relation $V(t)=L\dot I(t)$, i.e. each terminal potential is the rate of change of the branch flux linkage $\Phi=L I$; the capacitive branches obey $V=C^{-1}Q$ (in the scalar case $V_\beta=Q_\beta/C_{\beta\beta}$); the resistive branches obey $V=RI$, the circuit form of the Ohmic relation of [[post-em-material-closure]]; and the network laws are Kirchhoff's current law at each node and loop voltage balance around each independent loop. The circuit-level bookkeeping quantities of the model are the flux linkage $LI$ and the stored energies $\tfrac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$ and $\tfrac12Q^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}Q$.

(c) [Quasistatic regime declaration] The description is confined to configurations whose largest geometric extent $\ell$ and shortest time scale $T$ of interest satisfy the quasistatic smallness condition $\ell/(cT)\ll1$, with negligible radiation and negligible leakage and with specified conductor geometry and ideal terminals. The inequality is a declared regime of validity of the model; no error bound for an arbitrary full Maxwell solution follows from it alone, and the model does not assert that every asymptotically small configuration is described to any particular accuracy.

(d) [Status, units and scope] This is an adopted reduced model, not a deduction from the vacuum Maxwell equations; the matrices $L,C,R$ are model data, no microscopic constitutive law beyond the adopted branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] is asserted, and no radiation, distributed-element, nonlinear, hysteretic, leakage or proximity effect is included. SI units consistent with [[def-em-si-conventions]] are used: $V$ in volts, $I$ in amperes, $Q$ in coulombs, $t$ in seconds, $L$ in henries ($\mathrm H=\mathrm V\,\mathrm s\,\mathrm A^{-1}$), $C$ in farads ($\mathrm F=\mathrm C\,\mathrm V^{-1}$) and $R$ in ohms ($\Omega=\mathrm V\,\mathrm A^{-1}$). Where conductor matter moves, material speeds are subluminal, $|v|<c$, when the relativistic force interpretation is used.
item.strategy: An adopted nonproof formulation; no derivation is supplied and none is claimed. The objects are those of the framework: the laboratory region and time interval of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], the compact smooth conserved-current class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), and the Ohmic branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]. The list of essential elementary idealisations is explicit: fixed branch geometry, ideal terminals, negligible radiation and leakage, a declared quasistatic smallness condition, and constant branch matrices. Clause (d) records that the reduction is a model assumption and that $L,C,R$ carry no microscopic or empirical content. Source/scope review covers the formulation, the quasistatic qualification and the non-derivation; the accompanying theorems of this page derive conditional consequences of the adopted model only.

item.title: Linear flux linkage, reciprocal mutual inductance and magnetic energy of compact smooth conserved currents
item.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $j_1,\dots,j_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}j_\alpha=0$ be fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. Fix amplitudes $I\in\mathbb R^n$, put $J_I:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nI_\alpha j_\alpha$, let $A_{J_I}$ be the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential of [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] applied to the conserved current $J_I$, and let $B_{J_I}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}$. Define the linkage coefficients
$$L_{\alpha\beta}:=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\alpha,\beta=1,\dots,n .$$
Then:
(a) [Finiteness and self-energy] every $L_{\alpha\beta}$ is a finite real number: the defining double integral converges absolutely, and in particular every self-coefficient $L_{\alpha\alpha}$ is finite, so the compact smooth profiles carry a finite self-energy. This is a statement about the smooth profiles only; no finite value is assigned to a zero-radius thin-wire self-inductance.
(b) [Reciprocity and flux linkage] $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta$; $A_{J_I}=\sum_{\alpha}I_\alpha A_{j_\alpha}$ componentwise; and for every $\beta$ the linkage integral is
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nL_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha .$$
Thus the numbers $L_{\alpha\beta}$ are the linkage coefficients of the profiles: the linkage of profile $\beta$ with the field of the superposition is the linear combination $\sum_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha$.
(c) [Magnetic energy and positivity] with $U(I):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3$,
$$U(I)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^nL_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
all quantities finite; moreover $U(I)=0$ holds precisely when $J_I=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Consequently the symmetric matrix $L=(L_{\alpha\beta})$ is positive semidefinite, and it is positive definite exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent, i.e. when $\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha\equiv0$ forces $I=0$.
(d) [Scope] the theorem concerns fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles and their Coulomb-gauge fields. It asserts no thin-wire, sheet or singular self-inductance; no time-dependent, moving, radiating or material configuration; and no uniqueness of the vector potential. The identification of these coefficients with the inductance matrix of the adopted lumped circuit model, and of the linkage derivatives with terminal voltages, belongs to [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] and to the motional-emf result of this page, not to the field computation itself.
item.strategy: **Proof technique:** the Fubini/symmetry lemma [[lem-em-newtonian-linkage-symmetry]], the curl-field energy identity [[lem-em-newtonian-curl-field-energy]], and the Fubini representation of the linkage integrals. 1.1 Components: $j_\alpha$ is smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, so [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] applied to $J_I$ (equivalently to each $j_\alpha$, whose sum is $J_I$) gives $A_{J_I}\in C^\infty$, $\operatorname{div}A_{J_I}=0$, $-\Delta A_{J_I}=\mu_0J_I$ and $B_{J_I}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}$ with $\operatorname{div}B_{J_I}=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B_{J_I}=\mu_0J_I$ pointwise; by linearity of the Lebesgue integral ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[def-newtonian-potential]]) $A_{J_I}=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha A_{j_\alpha}$ with $A_{j_\alpha}$ the potentials of the individual profiles. 1.2 [[lem-em-newtonian-linkage-symmetry]] applied to $(u,v)=(j_\alpha,j_\beta)$ shows that each $L_{\alpha\beta}$ is a finite real number given by the absolutely convergent double integral and that $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$; applied to $(j_\beta,J_I)$ it gives $\int\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle=\mu_0\sum_\alpha I_\alpha\,(4\pi)^{-1}\iint\langle j_\beta(x),j_\alpha(y)\rangle/|x-y|=\sum_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha$, which is clause (b). 1.3 By the same symmetry, $\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\mu_0\int\langle J_I,NJ_I\rangle$, hence ([[lem-em-newtonian-curl-field-energy]] applied to the divergence-free current $J_I$ with parameter $\mu_0$) $U(I)=\frac12\int\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}|^2\ge0$, the integrals being finite by the same lemma; this is the energy identity of (c). 1.4 Vanishing: if $U(I)=0$ then $\int|B_{J_I}|^2=0$, and since $|B_{J_I}|^2$ is continuous and nonnegative, [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]] gives $|B_{J_I}|=0$ almost everywhere ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]); continuity then forces $B_{J_I}=0$ everywhere (otherwise $|B_{J_I}|$ would exceed a positive constant on a ball of positive measure by [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]] and [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}=\nabla\operatorname{div}A_{J_I}-\Delta A_{J_I}=\mu_0J_I$ ([[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]) vanishes, so $J_I=0$; conversely $J_I=0$ gives $A_{J_I}=0$ and $U(I)=0$. Symmetry of $L$ and the vanishing criterion give the stated positive-definiteness characterisation. Countable Choice is inherited from the magnetostatic vector-potential theorem and the Newtonian and Lebesgue supplier interfaces.

item.title: Restricted inductor energy LI^2/2 and its identification with the frozen magnetic field energy
item.statement:
Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) for clause (b), where it is inherited from the linkage suppliers.

(a) [Terminal-energy bookkeeping] Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]), let $t_0,t_1\in J$, let $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be constant and symmetric, let $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ (regularity on a non-open interval is read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention: the map extends to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$), and let $V(t):=L\dot I(t)$ be the terminal-voltage vector of the inductive branches as adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] (the Faraday branch: the terminal voltage of a branch is the rate of change of its flux linkage $\Phi=LI$). Then
$$\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle ,$$
and for $n=1$ with $L>0$ this reads $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}V I\,dt=\frac12L\bigl(I(t_1)^2-I(t_0)^2\bigr)$: the accumulated terminal energy equals the change of the inductor bookkeeping energy $\frac12LI^2$. The identity is exact for every $C^1$ current and fixed geometry; it uses only symmetry of $L$, the product rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus. For a changing geometry the mechanical work done on the circuit is an additional term and is not covered here.

(b) [Identification with the frozen field energy] Suppose in addition that the currents are realized by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), with instantaneous source $J(t):=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha(t)j_\alpha$, and that the inductance matrix is the linkage matrix of those profiles in the sense of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]: $L_{\alpha\beta}=\mu_0(4\pi)^{-1}\iint\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle/|x-y|$. Then for every $t\in J$
$$\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J(t),A_{J(t)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J(t)}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
the magnetic field energy of the frozen instantaneous configuration, and the terminal energy of (a) is the change of this field energy between $t_0$ and $t_1$. The relation between terminal voltages and flux derivatives is the content of [[pthm-em-motional-emf]]; the identification of the model's inductance matrix with the smooth-profile linkage matrix is part of the adopted model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]].

(c) [Scope] no radiation, distributed-element, material-loss, moving-geometry or thin-wire self-inductance claim is made; the frozen-configuration energy is not asserted to be the energy of a time-dependent full Maxwell solution.
item.strategy: **Proof technique:** product rule plus the fundamental theorem of calculus for (a); the reciprocity theorem for (b). 1.1 The quadratic function $W(I)=\frac12\langle I,LI\rangle$ is differentiable with $D W(I)\dot I=\langle L\dot I,I\rangle$ for symmetric $L$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); equivalently $\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}W(I(t))=\langle\dot I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\langle L\dot I(t),I(t)\rangle=\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle$. 1.2 Since $t\mapsto\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle$ is continuous and equals the derivative of the $C^1$ function $W\circ I$ on the interval $J$, the fundamental theorem of calculus in its second form ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]) gives the displayed integral identity of (a). For $n=1$ the quadratic form is $L I^2/2$ by inspection. 1.3 Clause (b) is [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]](c) applied to the profiles $j_\alpha$ and amplitudes $I(t)$ at each fixed $t$, combined with (a); the frozen instantaneous source is a legitimate input to the magnetostatic theorem at each time, and no time derivative of the fields is taken. 1.4 The mechanical-work caveat and the scope restrictions are those of the adopted model; the motional-emf theorem supplies the physical reading of the terminal voltage as a flux derivative, and no claim on a time-dependent Maxwell solution is made. Countable Choice is required only in clause (b), inherited through the linkage theorem.

item.title: Restricted RL decay and LC oscillation under the adopted circuit model
item.statement:
Let the lumped circuit model and its units be those of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $t_0\in J$; regularity on a non-open interval is read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention (extendability to a $C^k$ map on an open interval containing $J$). Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]], for the identification of the capacitive energy with the two-conductor electrostatic energy of [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] in clause (b), where it is inherited from that theorem; the other clauses use no choice principle. The inductive energy is that of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]].

(a) [RL circuit] Let $L>0$ and $R\ge0$ be constants and let $V:J\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then the initial value problem
$$L\dot I(t)+R\,I(t)=V(t),\qquad I(t_0)=I_0\in\mathbb R,$$
has exactly one $C^1$ solution on $J$, namely
$$I(t)=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)\Bigl[I_0+\frac1L\int_{t_0}^{t}\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{R(s-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)V(s)\,ds\Bigr],$$
and along it the inductive bookkeeping energy satisfies the power identity
$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigl(\frac12LI(t)^2\Bigr)=L\dot I(t)I(t)=V(t)I(t)-R\,I(t)^2 ,$$
i.e. the terminal power splits into the rate of change of the inductive energy and the Ohmic term $RI^2$. (For $R=0$ the same formula reduces to $I=I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^tV$.)

(b) [LC oscillation] Let $L>0$, $C>0$ and set $\Omega:=(LC)^{-1/2}>0$, $z_0:=Q_0-\mathrm i\,I_0/\Omega$, $w(t):=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))$ with the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]], and $Q(t):=\operatorname{Re}w(t)$. Then $Q$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, $Q(t_0)=Q_0$, $Q'(t_0)=I_0$, and
$$L\,Q''(t)+\frac{Q(t)}{C}=0\qquad\text{on }J ;$$
equivalently, with the real trigonometric functions of [[thm-eulers-formula]],
$$Q(t)=Q_0\cos\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac{I_0}{\Omega}\sin\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr).$$
Moreover the total bookkeeping energy
$$E(t):=\frac12L\,Q'(t)^2+\frac{Q(t)^2}{2C}$$
satisfies $E'(t)=Q'(t)\bigl(LQ''(t)+Q(t)/C\bigr)=0$ on $J$, hence $E$ is constant with value $\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$: the capacitive term $\frac12Q^2/C$ is the two-conductor electrostatic energy of [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] and the inductive term $\frac12LI^2$ is that of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]], so in the lossless loop the total stored bookkeeping energy is conserved.

(c) [Scope] both statements are consequences of the expressly adopted circuit reduction, with the sign conventions and relations of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; they assert no general network completeness, no derivation from the full time-dependent Maxwell system, no radiation or distributed-element effect and no empirical claim.
item.strategy:
**Proof technique:** the published integrating-factor theorem for (a); an explicit complex-exponential candidate verified by differentiation and an energy-conservation comparison for (b).

1.1 (a) With $p:=R/L$ constant and $q:=V/L$ continuous on $J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]), the integrating factor theorem [[thm-first-order-linear-ode-integrating-factor]] gives existence, uniqueness of the $C^1$ solution of the IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] and exactly the displayed formula. The power identity is the product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) applied to $\frac12LI^2$ together with the circuit equation.

1.2 (b) The map $w$ is the restriction to the real interval $J$ of the entire function $z\mapsto z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(z-t_0))$; the complex exponential is entire with derivative itself ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), the affine map is complex-linear, so the algebra and chain rules for complex derivatives ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]]) give $w'=\mathrm i\Omega w$ and $w''=(\mathrm i\Omega)^2w=-\Omega^2w$ on $J$; complex differentiability implies real differentiability with the complex-linear derivative ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]) and the real chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) gives the corresponding real derivatives of the components. Taking real parts, $Q=\operatorname{Re}w$ is $C^2$ with $Q'=\operatorname{Re}w'$ and $Q''=\operatorname{Re}w''=-\Omega^2Q$, which is $LQ''+Q/C=0$ because $\Omega^2=1/(LC)$; moreover $w(t_0)=Q_0-\mathrm iI_0/\Omega$ gives $Q(t_0)=Q_0$ and $Q'(t_0)=\operatorname{Re}(\mathrm i\Omega z_0)=I_0$. 1.3 (b) The energy identity is the product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) applied to $E$: $E'=LQ'Q''+QQ'/C=Q'(LQ''+Q/C)=0$ by the equation of the previous step. Since $E$ is continuous on the interval $J$ with vanishing derivative at every interior point, [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]] gives $E\equiv E(t_0)=\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$. item.title: Sliding bar on fixed rails: motional emf and mechanical-electrical power balance
item.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) where it is inherited from the transport supplier below. Idealised setup, all in the laboratory frame and units of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix $l>0$, $B_0\ge0$, an interval $J$ and a $C^1$ function $x:J\to[a_0,a_1]$ with $a_0<a_1$, $x(t)\in(a_0,a_1)$ for all $t$ and $|x'(t)|<c$. Let the material circuit of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]] be the rigid rectangular circuit whose two rails are the segments $\{(s,\pm l/2,0):s\in[a_0,a_1]\}$ at rest, whose left side is the fixed segment $\{(a_0,w,0):|w|\le l/2\}$ at rest, and whose bar at time $t$ is the segment $\{(x(t),w,0):|w|\le l/2\}$, moving with material velocity $v(t)=x'(t)e_1$ on the bar and zero elsewhere; the bar is rigid and slides on the rails without friction. The electromagnetic field is the declared external field $E=0$, $B=B_0e_3$ on $\mathbb R^3$ (fields produced by the circuit itself are neglected); the bar is a straight homogeneous conductor of length $l$ and cross-section area $A>0$ carrying the lumped current $I(t)$ with uniform current density $J(t)=(I(t)/A)e_2$ on the bar; the rails and the closing side carry the same lumped current but have zero material velocity.

Then, with the boundary orientation induced by the circuit's parametrisation (so that the enclosed normal is $e_3$ and the bar is traversed in the $+e_2$ direction):
(a) [Motional emf] the flux is $\Phi(t)=B_0\,l\,(x(t)-a_0)$ and the electromotive force of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]] is
$$\mathrm{emf}(t)=-B_0\,l\,x'(t),$$
so at speed $v=|x'|$ the magnitude is $|\mathrm{emf}|=B_0lv$, with the sign fixed by the orientation and by the sign of $x'$
(b) [Force on the bar] the total electromagnetic force on the bar, evaluated with the continuum force density of the adopted coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], is the absolutely convergent integral
$$F(t)=\int_{\text{bar}}J(t)\times B\,d\lambda_3=I(t)\,l\,e_2\times B_0e_3=I(t)B_0l\,e_1$$
([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]);
(c) [Power balance] at every $t$, the mechanical power $F(t)\cdot v(t)$ delivered by the field to the bar and the electrical power $\mathrm{emf}(t)I(t)$ delivered by the emf to the circuit satisfy the exact identity
$$F(t)\cdot v(t)+\mathrm{emf}(t)\,I(t)=I(t)B_0lv(t)-B_0lv(t)I(t)=0 ;$$
in the ideal model the device converts between mechanical and electrical power with no dissipation and no radiation.
(d) [Scope] a hypothetical idealised computation under the stated assumptions, with no measurement: the motion $x$ is prescribed (no bar dynamics is derived), self-fields, radiation, friction, contact resistance, conductor deformation and any material constitutive law beyond the ideal conductor are neglected, and the model is exactly the one stated; it is not asserted that a physical apparatus realises these idealisations.

after.title: Sliding bar on fixed rails: motional emf and mechanical-electrical power balance
after.statement:
Assume AComega for the explicitly used Lebesgue bar-volume interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Work in the laboratory frame and units of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix $l>0$, $B_0\ge0$, a nonempty interval $J$ with a specified $C^1$ neighbourhood extension for motion and its velocity jets when $J$ is not open (in particular singleton data are read through that supplied extension), and prescribed $C^1$ motion $x:J\to(a_0,a_1)$ with $a_0<a_1$ and $|x'(t)|<c$. The fixed rails have centerlines $(s,\pm l/2,0)$, $a_0\le s\le a_1$, and the left closing side is $(a_0,w,0)$, $|w|\le l/2$. At time $t$ the ideal oriented contour $C(t)$ comprises only the rail portions $a_0\le s\le x(t)$, that left side, and the sliding bar centerline $(x(t),w,0)$. Give it normal $e_3$, hence traverse the bar in the $+e_2$ direction. The rails and closing side have material velocity zero; the bar velocity is $v_b(t)=x'(t)e_1$. These are separate segment velocities with sliding contacts; endpoint values at the contacts are taken independently on each segment. Define the contact-model emf as the sum of its four segment integrals $\sum_\gamma\int_\gamma(E+v_\gamma\times B)\cdot dr$ in [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. This is not a single-valued smooth moving material sheet of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]]. The external test field is $E=0$, $B=B_0e_3$; all self-fields are neglected.

For force bookkeeping choose an actual finite-volume homogeneous bar, separate from the ideal centerline: fix $d,h>0$ with cross-section area $A=dh$ and set $K_t=[x(t)-d/2,x(t)+d/2]\times[-l/2,l/2]\times[-h/2,h/2]$, so $\lambda_3(K_t)=Al$. For each frozen time prescribe the uniform current density $j_t=(I(t)/A)e_2$ on its interior, with the ideal local conductor-matter coupling of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) applied there. Its extension to the boundary is used only for the volume integral; contacts/end faces have zero volume and no additional contact force is included. The same signed lumped current runs around the contour. The local force-law adoption and prescribed current do not assert a total Maxwell or matter-dynamical solution.

(a) The rectangular flux is $\Phi(t)=B_0l(x(t)-a_0)$ and the segmentwise emf is $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-B_0lx'(t)=-\Phi'(t)$. Its magnitude is $B_0l|x'|$, including either motion direction and $B_0=0$.
(b) The finite-volume force is
$$F(t)=\int_{K_t}j_t\times B\,d\lambda_3=I(t)B_0l e_1.$$
(c) The signed instantaneous balance is
$$F(t)\cdot v_b(t)+\mathrm{emf}(t)I(t)=I(t)B_0lx'(t)-B_0lx'(t)I(t)=0.$$
It is ideal mechanical/electrical transfer bookkeeping with prescribed motion and current; no dissipative, radiation or field-storage term is included. A support enforcing the motion may supply the opposite mechanical power.
(d) This is a hypothetical conditional sliding-contact model with no measurement. Self-fields, radiation, friction, contact resistance, deformation and constitutive details are neglected; no bar equation of motion, physical realization, or total Maxwell solution is asserted. The strict $C^2$ material-sheet theorem remains a separate result under its own hypotheses.
after.strategy: At each frozen time the four segments are ordinary affine paths. The three resting segments contribute zero because $E=0$ and their material velocity is zero. This is the prescribed local continuum matter coupling, not a force inferred for an arbitrary source without such a matter model. (c) uses the signed velocity vector $v_b=x'e_1$ in the Euclidean dot product, giving exactly $IB_0lx'-B_0lx'I=0$, even when $I$ or $x'$ is negative or zero. The centerline is a contour for emf and has zero three-dimensional volume; the force integral is over $K_t$. Nothing here supplies the neglected self-field or a smooth global current through the sliding contacts. item.title: Two-circuit mutual inductance, the perfect-linkage bound and ideal-transformer limitations
item.statement:
Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $L=\begin{pmatrix}L_1&M\\M&L_2\end{pmatrix}$ be a constant symmetric block of its inductance matrix with $L_1,L_2>0$. Let $I_1,I_2:J\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ currents on an interval $J$ with terminal voltages $V_\alpha=\sum_\beta L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\beta$. Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the realization and bounded-linking clauses (b), where it is inherited from the linkage and energy suppliers.

(a) [Energy and instantaneous power] the stored inductive bookkeeping energy is
$$W(t)=\tfrac12L_1I_1(t)^2+\tfrac12L_2I_2(t)^2+MI_1(t)I_2(t),$$
and $V_1I_1+V_2I_2=\dot W$ by part (a) of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]]; the mutual term increases the energy for currents of the same sign and decreases it for opposite signs (as the sign of the product $I_1I_2$ indicates when $M>0$).

(b) [Perfect linkage and the bound] if the two currents are realised by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b) with linkage matrix $L$ as in [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]], then $W(t)\ge0$ for all currents, and evaluating the quadratic form on $(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ gives the bound
$$|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2};$$
moreover if $M^2=L_1L_2$ (perfect linkage) then the null direction $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ has $J_I=0$ pointwise by the vanishing clause of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]](c).

(c) [Ideal common-flux model] if $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, choose any $\Lambda>0$ and set $N_1:=\sqrt{L_1/\Lambda}$, $N_2:=\sqrt{L_2/\Lambda}$; then $L_1=\Lambda N_1^2$, $L_2=\Lambda N_2^2$ and $M=\Lambda N_1N_2$. Writing $\Phi_c:=\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)$ for the common flux linkage, the terminal voltages are
$$V_1=N_1\dot\Phi_c,\qquad V_2=N_2\dot\Phi_c,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{V_1}{N_1}=\frac{V_2}{N_2}=\dot\Phi_c,$$
and the stored energy is $W=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$; equivalently the induced emfs $e_\alpha:=-V_\alpha$ satisfy $e_1/N_1=e_2/N_2=-\dot\Phi_c$. This is the explicitly adopted common-linkage ('ideal transformer') model with turns ratio $N_1:N_2$.

(d) [Limitations] if the linkage is imperfect then $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ and the exact voltage-ratio relations fail; winding resistance, hysteresis and core loss, stray capacitance, magnetising current and finite permeability are outside the declared model and are not inferred from it. No measurement is involved; the statements are conditional computations in the ideal model.
item.strategy: **Verification.** (a) is the two-dimensional instance of the quadratic form and power identity of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]](a), together with the product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). (b) is [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]](c) applied to the two profiles: $W(t)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta\ge0$, and substituting $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ gives $W=\frac12L_1L_2+\frac12L_2L_1-M\sqrt{L_1L_2}=L_1L_2-M\sqrt{L_1L_2}\ge0$, i.e. $M\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; substituting the opposite sign gives the lower bound, hence $|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$. If $M^2=L_1L_2$ then that substitution yields $W=0$, so the associated current $J_I$ vanishes pointwise by the vanishing clause of the same theorem. (c) With $N_1,N_2,\Lambda$ as defined, $L_1=\Lambda N_1^2$ and $L_2=\Lambda N_2^2$ by construction and $M=\Lambda N_1N_2$ because $\sqrt{\Lambda N_1^2\cdot\Lambda N_2^2}=\Lambda N_1N_2$; hence $V_1=L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2=\Lambda N_1(N_1\dot I_1+N_2\dot I_2)=N_1\dot\Phi_c$ and likewise $V_2=N_2\dot\Phi_c$, while $W=\frac12\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)^2=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$ by direct expansion. The sign convention is the terminal-voltage convention of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the physically induced emfs are the negatives, as in the moving-loop result, which is why the stated ratios carry the common minus sign. (d) records the model boundaries; the example asserts nothing about a physical transformer and involves no measurement. Countable Choice is used only through the realization clauses (b) and is inherited from [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]] and [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]].

item.title: Exponential RL response under a constant terminal voltage
item.statement:
In the RL branch of [[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]] with the declared units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let the source voltage be the constant $V_0\in\mathbb R$, let $R>0$ and $L>0$, and let $t_0\in J$ and $I_0\in\mathbb R$. Then the unique $C^1$ solution of $L\dot I+RI=V_0$, $I(t_0)=I_0$, is
$$I(t)=\frac{V_0}{R}+\Bigl(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\Bigr)\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr),\qquad t\in J .$$
In particular the deviation decays exponentially, $|I(t)-V_0/R|=|I_0-V_0/R|\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$, with time constant $\tau=L/R$, and if $J$ is unbounded above then $I(t)\to V_0/R$ as $t\to+\infty$; $I\equiv V_0/R$ is the unique stationary solution; and the transient part is the free decay $\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ of the initial deviation $I_0-V_0/R$. The computation is conditional on the adopted lumped model, constant elements and fixed geometry; no measurement is involved.
item.strategy: **Verification.** The function $t\mapsto\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ is differentiable with derivative $-(R/L)\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ by the chain rule for the affine substitution in the real exponential ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). Substituting the displayed $I$ gives $\dot I=-(R/L)(I_0-V_0/R)\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$, hence $L\dot I+RI=V_0$ identically, and $I(t_0)=V_0/R+(I_0-V_0/R)=I_0$. Uniqueness of this solution within the RL theorem [[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]](a) is inherited from the published integrating-factor theorem; the limit statement is the elementary fact that the exponential term tends to $0$ as $(t-t_0)\to+\infty$ and the special case $I_0=V_0/R$ is constant. after.title: Exponential RL response under a constant terminal voltage
after.statement:
In the RL branch of [[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]] with the declared units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let the source voltage be the constant $V_0\in\mathbb R$, let $R>0$ and $L>0$, and let $t_0\in J$ and $I_0\in\mathbb R$. Then the unique $C^1$ solution of $L\dot I+RI=V_0$, $I(t_0)=I_0$, is
$$I(t)=\frac{V_0}{R}+\Bigl(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\Bigr)\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr),\qquad t\in J .$$
In particular the deviation decays exponentially, $|I(t)-V_0/R|=|I_0-V_0/R|\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$, with time constant $\tau=L/R$, and if $J$ is unbounded above then $I(t)\to V_0/R$ as $t\to+\infty$; $I\equiv V_0/R$ is the unique stationary solution; and the transient part is the free decay $\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ of the initial deviation $I_0-V_0/R$. The computation is conditional on the adopted lumped model, constant elements and fixed geometry; no measurement is involved.
after.strategy: **Verification.** The function $t\mapsto\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ is differentiable with derivative $-(R/L)\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ by the chain rule for the affine substitution in the real exponential ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). Substituting the displayed $I$ gives $\dot I=-(R/L)(I_0-V_0/R)\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$, hence $L\dot I+RI=V_0$ identically, and $I(t_0)=V_0/R+(I_0-V_0/R)=I_0$. Uniqueness of this solution within the RL theorem [[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]](a) is inherited from the published integrating-factor theorem; the limit statement follows from [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]] since $-R(t-t_0)/L\to-\infty$ on a time interval unbounded above and the special case $I_0=V_0/R$ is constant. No claim beyond the ideal model is made.

item.title: Laboratory geometry: a restricted inertial chart, its spatial slices and fixed-time fields
item.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the laboratory time coordinate $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the laboratory position $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed. (c) [Laboratory fields] A laboratory field of rank $m$ is a map $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$, $p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class $C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed $t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is asserted beyond the class stated for it. (d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer field is defined here.
item.strategy: A construction definition with elementary verifications. The inertial chart $x$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] is a bijection, so its restriction to the set of events whose chart coordinates lie in $cI\times\Omega$ has image $cI\times\Omega$; composing with the bijection $cI\times\Omega\to I\times\Omega$, $(ct,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ (bijective because $c>0$) gives the bijection $\Phi$. Each slice $U_t$ is $\Phi^{-1}(\{t\}\times\Omega)$, on which $r$ restricts to a bijection onto $\Omega$. The claims about $n$, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, $\delta$ and the orientation are exactly the content of [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]; the $C^k$ notion is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] and the two kinds of partial derivative are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] applied to the product coordinates. Clause (d) records conventions only: the frame dependence of $r,\delta$ and slices is stated rather than hidden, and no Galilean or observer-congruence claim is made. Nothing here uses a theorem of the framework, and the laboratory region may be a proper subset of $A$; no global chart of $A$ other than the given inertial chart is asserted.

item.title: The electric and magnetic fields as fixed-time spatial vector fields
item.statement: Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An electric field of class $C^k$ on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a magnetic field of class $C^k$ is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses: $C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and no regularity beyond it is asserted. Conventions: (a) $E$ is a polar vector and $B$ an axial vector relative to the orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] are proper and orientation preserving, so orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them; (b) the fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at a point of singular source support is asserted; (c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T; (d) the identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] and is not presupposed here.
item.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition: the fields are maps on the product $\Omega\times I$ of the laboratory region with a stated class of regularity, and their fixed-time readings are spatial vector fields in the frame basis. The regularity notion is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; the polar/axial convention and the exclusion of pointwise values at singular source support are conventions recorded explicitly rather than used implicitly. No differential equation and no derived quantity is introduced by this definition.

item.title: Framework-local SI units, the vacuum constants and the exact/measured status of their values
item.statement: Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted (the pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate/uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value); the electric constant is defined within the framework by $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of [[def-em-sources]] carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ carries kg m s$^{-1}$ ([[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]); field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI, they do not by themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light, which is the physical adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]].
item.strategy: A convention definition: it fixes the coordinate normalisation $x^0=ct$, the unit of each quantity used in this framework, the exact SI defining values of $c$ and $e$ and the measured status of $\mu_0$. The exact values $c=299\,792\,458$ m/s and $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and the statements that the new definition of the ampere fixes $e$ rather than $\mu_0$, that $\mu_0$ must now be determined experimentally, and that $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$ remains exact, are taken from the SI brochure's defining-constants table and its ampere section. The framework's definition of $\varepsilon_0$ by $(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ is a definition consistent with that exact relation; the uncertainty carried by $\varepsilon_0$ is recorded rather than hidden. The dimensional checks of the framework's equations and couplings are developed on the companion examples page of this pair. No exact or current measured numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted and no experiment is claimed. The historical nominal and adoption uncertainty are explicitly source context, not a substitution for the current experimentally determined constant.

item.title: Moving parametrized surface patches and their flux
item.statement: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a compact finite elementary Green region with its positive boundary orientation and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval. Let $r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ extend to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior, and require the images to be embedded if an actual material sheet is intended. Define the velocity $v$ on a neighbourhood of the swept surface by $v(r(u,v,t),t):=\partial_tr(u,v,t)$, requiring it to be single-valued and of class $C^1$. For a $C^1$ field $B$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the flux through the patch at time $t$ is $$\Phi(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(u,v,t),t),\,r_u(u,v,t)\times r_v(u,v,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dv.$$
item.strategy: Elementary Green regions are compact Jordan-measurable parameter regions, so the flux is a Riemann integral, and the orientation is the patch orientation of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. Single-valuedness of the velocity is the hypothesis that makes the transport formula of the moving-flux lemma well posed. No physical assertion is made.

item.title: Newtonian potential of smooth compact data is smooth and solves the Poisson equation pointwise
item.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and let $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dy .$$ Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ the spatial derivative satisfies $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. In particular, for smooth compactly supported $\rho$ the field $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth. The statement is about the explicit integral transform of compactly supported smooth data and does not assume smoothness of the kernel at the pole; the distributional identity $-\Delta Nf=f$ is the one supplied by the Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]), upgraded here from a distributional to a pointwise identity for smooth data.
item.strategy: Substitute $z=x-y$: $Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)f(x-z)\,dz$ with $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. On a compact set of $x$ the derivatives $D^\alpha f(x-z)$ vanish outside a common bounded $z$-set and are bounded there, so every parameter derivative has an integrable bound $C|\Phi|$ on that set; differentiation under the integral sign ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]], applied coordinatewise) gives $D^\alpha Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)D^\alpha f(x-z)\,dz$ and continuity of the result, hence $C^\infty$. The distributional identity $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ is the cited Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]). Since both sides are smooth functions (the right side is $f$, the left side is a smooth representative by the first part), the distributional equality is a pointwise equality by localization against compactly supported nonnegative smooth tests. The derivative identity $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$ is the parameter-differentiation formula just proved, and the final smoothness claim for $E$ follows by linearity. Countable Choice is inherited from the exact Statement of [[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]] and its regular-distribution interface; it is explicitly assumed here, not silently removed by the smooth upgrade.

item.title: The far-field gradient of a compactly supported Newtonian potential
item.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the Lebesgue interface used below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge3$, let $\Phi$ be the fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ on $\mathbb R^n$ normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]), so that for $z\ne0$
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{|z|^{2-n}}{(n-2)\omega_{n-1}},\qquad \nabla\Phi(z)=-\frac{z}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^n},\qquad |\nabla\Phi(z)|=\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^{n-1}},$$
let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ be real, measurable and zero $\lambda_n$-almost everywhere outside a closed ball $\overline B_R(0)=\{x:|x|\le R\}$ of finite radius $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$$
be the Newtonian potential ([[def-newtonian-potential]]). Then:
(a) [Representation and differentiability off the far field] for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $|x|>2R$ the integral $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$ is absolutely convergent, the function $Nf$ is differentiable at $x$ with
$$\nabla(Nf)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y),$$
and $x\mapsto\nabla(Nf)(x)$ is continuous on the open set $\{x:|x|>2R\}$;
(b) [Decay bound] for every $x$ with $|x|>2R$,
$$|\nabla(Nf)(x)|\le\frac{2^{n-1}\|f\|_1}{\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}},\qquad \|f\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|f|\,d\lambda_n;$$
(c) [Scope] the hypothesis is compact support together with $L^1$-integrability; no boundedness of $f$ is assumed, and nothing is asserted at points with $|x|\le2R$ (where the kernel singularity may meet the support of $f$).
item.strategy: Fix $x_0$ with $|x_0|>2R$ and choose $0<\delta<|x_0|-2R$. On the full open ball $U=B_\delta(x_0)$, every $y\in\overline B_R$ obeys $|x-y|\ge |x_0|-\delta-R=:c>0$. Thus both $|\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\le c^{2-n}|f(y)|/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ and $|\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\le c^{1-n}|f(y)|/\omega_{n-1}$ hold throughout $U$, outside the single null set on which $f$ may fail to vanish off $\overline B_R$. Equivalently reset $f$ to zero on that set without changing any integral. The majorants are integrable; the kernel and its coordinate derivatives are continuous off zero and their products with measurable $f$ are measurable ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Restricting to each sufficiently short coordinate interval through any $x\in U$, [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] yields $\partial_iNf(x)=\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)dy$. For any sequence $x_m\to x$ in $U$, the derivative integrands converge almost everywhere and have the same full-neighbourhood majorant $c^{1-n}|f|/\omega_{n-1}$. [[thm-dominated-convergence]] therefore proves continuity of each partial derivative as a function of all coordinates on $U$, not merely along coordinate lines. [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]] now gives total differentiability and the displayed gradient representation; the continuous vector of partials is the gradient ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). As $x_0$ was arbitrary, (a) holds throughout the stated far field. For (b), $|x-y|\ge |x|-R>|x|/2$ on the support, so $|\nabla\Phi(x-y)|\le2^{n-1}/(\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1})$; integrating against $|f|$ gives the stated bound. No boundedness of $f$ or interior-support assertion is used. The support ball is measurable, and the choice cost is exactly the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the measure interfaces.

item.title: Charge parameter, frame charge and current densities, volume charge and flux, and the four-current
item.statement:
Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is not asserted. (b) [Smooth source fields] A smooth (volume) source field on $\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the frame charge density (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the frame current density (A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if $V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define $Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$ by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf1_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$
where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is defined through its positive and negative parts ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). This integral is absolutely finite, since $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on $\overline V$ and $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure. On the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption, $Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]. The empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal field $n_S$ the current flux at time $t$ is $\int_S J(y,t)\cdot n_S(y)\,dS$ ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them. (c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and $j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model, and hence the component transformation law of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts. This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents. (d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch] Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a $C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier $\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so $u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic convention is $j^0=c\rho$,
$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$
Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$, including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike $U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is $v^i:=cu^i$.
For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch, $U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and
$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$
Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model: in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$ (equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are retained. (e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.
item.strategy:
Keep clauses (a)-(c) as explicit source types and the adopted physical identification. The compact Jordan branch uses [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]] and [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]; flux uses [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. For the broader Lebesgue branch assume the explicitly stated Countable Choice, without Dependent Choice or a convergence/FTC assumption. Fix $t$ and an admitted nonempty $V$. The continuous function $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded by $M_t<\infty$ in absolute value on compact $\overline V$ by [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]. Its zero extension $F_t$ is Borel: for every open $O\subseteq\mathbb R$, the inverse image inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively open and hence open in $\mathbb R^3$; add the closed complement of $\Omega$ precisely when $0\in O$. This is also the open-set form of [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]. Under Countable Choice, Borel sets are Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]) and bounded measurable $V$ has finite measure ([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]). Positive/negative parts and their restrictions by $\mathbf1_V$ are measurable by [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. The bound $|F_t|\mathbf1_V\le M_t\mathbf1_V$ and [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] give
$$\int|F_t|\mathbf1_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty,$$
where the indicator integral is its simple-function value by [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]. This proves exactly the absolute signed integrability required by [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and defines $Q$ using the nonnegative restrictions of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]. For empty $V$ the product is zero. On compact Jordan $V$, the continuous density restricted to V has a bounded Borel zero extension to a bounding rectangle, so the exact compact-Jordan clause of [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], also under Countable Choice, identifies the two finite integral values. The algebraic supplier [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]](vii) gives $j=\rho_0U=\rho_0U^0u$; its coordinate density is $j^0$, whereas the present SI source convention defines $j^0=c\rho$. Division by $c>0$ gives $\rho=\rho_0U^0/c$ and $\rho-\rho_0=\rho_0(U^0-c)/c$, proving exactly the stated equality cases. The spatial components give $J^i=c\rho u^i$. Neither $U^0=c$ nor chart normalization $u^0=1$ is a proper-four-velocity condition.
In the additional normalized material model, write $v=c(U^1,U^2,U^3)/U^0$. The norm equation $-(U^0)^2+|U_{\mathrm{sp}}|^2=-c^2$ gives $(U^0)^2(1-|v|^2/c^2)=c^2$, and future timelikeness gives $U^0>0$ and $|v|<c$, so $U^0=c\gamma$. This is the exact four-velocity/relative-velocity content of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]; substitution gives $\rho=\gamma\rho_0$ and $J=\rho v$. In its comoving frame $U^0=c$, hence the source convention identifies the scalar multiplier with the stipulated rest-frame density. Since $\gamma=1$ if and only if $v=0$, the normalized equality cases follow, including $\rho_0=0$. All density readings remain within the adopted current model; no conservation, measurement, general current factorization, force law or singular-source regularity is deduced.
